messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Arthur, a 66-year-old software engineer, presented with a quiet, reserved demeanor, his movements precise and deliberate. For decades, he had carried the weight of a childhood marked by an unpredictable terror. He remembered clearly the icy grip of his caregiver's hand, pressing down on his arm, or the burning sting of a ruler across his skin, each sensation searing itself into his memory. What remained most vivid was the relentless pounding of his own heart against his ribs during those moments, a frantic drumbeat of pure fear, making him feel trapped within his own body.

Now, any sudden change in temperature against his skin, be it a draft from an open window in his office or the cool metal of a doorknob, could instantly transport Arthur back, his mind flooded with the memory of that helpless child. Similarly, the simple awareness of his own heart racing, perhaps after climbing a flight of stairs or from a moment of surprise, would trigger an immediate and overwhelming sense of dread, as if danger were imminent. These intrusive memories would arrive unbidden, sharp and vivid, pulling him abruptly from his present reality into the past.

Over the years, Arthur had developed a deeply ingrained vigilance. He had come to believe that he had to be especially careful because you never knew what could happen next. This conviction drove him to constantly scan his surroundings, whether walking through a supermarket or sitting in his cubicle, for anything that could be construed as a potential weapon or dangerous object. He was certain that his body reacted to danger before his mind even had time to think, often experiencing a jolt of alarm or a surge of adrenaline in response to an innocuous sound or movement. This hyper-alertness was particularly pronounced when someone touched him unexpectedly; even his wife’s gentle hand on his shoulder would elicit a sharp, involuntary flinch, a sudden tightening of his muscles.

To manage these intense internal experiences, Arthur had adopted a series of strategies that had, over time, reshaped his life. He found himself actively avoiding paying attention to or looking at his own body, particularly his chest, as if by ignoring the physical sensations he could quell the rising panic. He also began to withdraw from social interactions, finding it increasingly difficult to see people he had socialized with before, even old friends from his software engineering firm. He had come to feel that he was permanently an outsider now, fundamentally different from others, and he held a profound mistrust, certain that people couldn't be trusted. This belief solidified his reluctance to engage.

The most profound impact was on his marriage. What frightened him most was his inability to tolerate any form of physical contact with others, including his wife. He would subtly shift away on the couch, find excuses to be in different rooms, or invent reasons to avoid holding hands. This avoidance had created an emotional chasm between them, leaving his wife feeling confused and rejected. At work, his once-collaborative spirit had waned. He preferred to work in isolation, declining team lunches and after-work gatherings, further solidifying his sense of being an outsider. His colleagues noticed his increasing aloofness, attributing it to his age or eccentricity, unaware of the internal battle he waged.

The cumulative effect of these avoidant behaviours and the constant internal tension had become unbearable. His wife, worried by his increasing withdrawal and the palpable distance between them, finally urged him to seek help. Arthur arrived at the clinic feeling utterly exhausted, trapped by his own caution and the ever-present threat of his past. He longed for relief from the constant vigilance and the gnawing sense of isolation, but what he feared most was that his body and mind were irrevocably broken, forever destined to react with alarm to the ghosts of his past.
